clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder from biallelic INSR mutations causing severe insulin resistance, intermediate in severity between Donohue syndrome and type A insulin resistance
Presents in childhood with growth impairment, acanthosis nigricans, coarse features, dental and nail dysplasia, and pineal hyperplasia in some patients
Extreme endogenous hyperinsulinaemia accompanies fasting hypoglycaemia and severe postprandial hyperglycaemia, reflecting defective receptor signalling
Diabetic ketoacidosis and difficult-to-control hyperglycaemia often develop as the child grows
Because the block is at the insulin receptor, escalating exogenous insulin is largely ineffective
Recombinant IGF-1 (with or without IGFBP-3) can engage the IGF-1 receptor to improve glycaemic control in these severe INSR defects
Longer survival than Donohue syndrome allows accumulation of chronic complications
Diagnosis rests on the phenotype, the fasting-hypoglycaemia/postprandial-hyperglycaemia pattern with extreme hyperinsulinaemia, and INSR genetics
reference.pathophysiology: Rabson-Mendenhall syndrome is caused by biallelic mutations in the insulin receptor gene (INSR) that severely, though not completely, impair receptor function. With markedly reduced insulin signalling, tissues cannot take up glucose or grow normally despite very high insulin levels, and hepatic glucose output is poorly suppressed. The result is severe insulin resistance manifest as fasting hypoglycaemia alternating with pronounced postprandial hyperglycaemia, together with acanthosis nigricans, growth impairment, and the characteristic dysmorphic, dental, and nail features. Because residual receptor function is greater than in Donohue syndrome, the course is less rapidly fatal but progresses to overt, ketosis-prone diabetes.
additionalDifferentials: Poorly controlled type 1 diabetes with acanthosis
Other syndromic causes of short stature with acanthosis nigricans
additionalInvestigations: Fasting and postprandial glucose to demonstrate the characteristic oscillation
Fasting insulin and C-peptide, markedly elevated
INSR gene sequencing to confirm biallelic mutations
HbA1c and ketone monitoring given ketoacidosis risk
Dental, skeletal, and pineal imaging where clinically indicated
Lipid profile and leptin to characterise the metabolic phenotype
redFlags: Diabetic ketoacidosis or severe uncontrolled hyperglycaemia
Progressive growth failure and metabolic decompensation
Emergence of chronic microvascular diabetic complications
reference.prognosis: Children with Rabson-Mendenhall syndrome generally survive longer than those with Donohue syndrome, often into the second decade or beyond, but face progressive, difficult-to-control diabetes with ketoacidosis and chronic complications; IGF-1-based therapy may improve control.
pitfalls: Interpreting extreme hyperinsulinaemia as an insulin-secreting tumour
Escalating exogenous insulin doses that fail to overcome receptor resistance
Attributing growth failure and acanthosis to obesity alone
Neglecting INSR genetic confirmation and family counselling
references: Endocrine Society clinical practice guidance on severe insulin resistance
management: Recombinant IGF-1, with or without IGFBP-3, to bypass the defective insulin receptor by signalling through the IGF-1 receptor and improve glycaemic control
Insulin sensitisers such as metformin and, where used, high-dose insulin, recognising that receptor-level blockade limits the benefit of exogenous insulin
A dietary strategy of frequent complex-carbohydrate feeds to blunt the swings between fasting hypoglycaemia and postprandial hyperglycaemia
Regular monitoring of glycaemic control and ketones given the ketosis-prone, difficult-to-control diabetes, together with surveillance for chronic complications
Prompt treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis with fluids, electrolyte correction and insulin during acute decompensation
Multidisciplinary follow-up with paediatric endocrinology, dietetics, and dental and growth surveillance
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder and testing of at-risk relatives
